data.title: Expedition to Polish hillforts – Kraków and Bnin (day 1)
data.excerpt: In October 2022, nine members of the Hradiská civic association set out for the hillforts of Poland and its earliest history, with the Polish open-air archaeological museums as their main goal. The first day took them to the archaeological museum in Kraków – where the famous Zbruch Idol turned out to be away for research and restoration – and on to the peninsula hillfort of Bnin.

children.text: In October 2022, nine of us members of the Hradiská civic association set out on an expedition in search of the hillforts of Poland and its earliest history. Our main goal was the open-air archaeological museums, which the Poles keep at an excellent standard, and on the way between them we also visited some interesting unreconstructed hillforts that lay along our route.

For the journey we used a borrowed red Little Red Riding Hood – an Opel Vivaro, which admittedly had its best years behind it, but had fairly comfortable seats and a large luggage space. Despite some initial mild mistrust, we came to understand each other quite well in the end and it accompanied us reliably throughout the whole long expedition.
The main point of the first day of the expedition was the archaeological museum in Kraków, which is supposed to hold the best-known “Slavic” idol, the so-called
. The city of Kraków has a very beautifully restored centre, as many of you certainly know. Its broad streets are slightly reminiscent of Paris and other interesting Western European cities.

children.text: is indeed very extensive and rich, with a great many exhibits. You will find beautiful finds here from the Palaeolithic right down to the Middle Ages, and we were surprised by the fairly extensive display from the period of ancient Egypt and from South America. The only real disappointment was to learn that the Zbruch Idol, which we had been very much looking forward to, is at present away from the museum and is undergoing research and restoration work. Even without it, however, I can warmly recommend the museum to anyone interested in archaeology and history.

After the visit to the museum and lunch, an unpleasant surprise awaited us in the form of a parking fine. The parking policy in Kraków is about as “welcoming” to foreign tourists as it is in Bratislava. It is quite a chaos, because in some parts of the city there are parking spaces together with ticket machines, yet it is often unclear where you may park for a fee and where not. And so we parked, politely paid the parking fee at the machine, and on our return the municipal police were waiting for us with a wheel clamp, and we were immediately 200 zloty lighter, because apparently only holders of special long-term parking cards may park for a fee in that place. At least it was exciting, though. It did not put us off further exploring.

children.text: Besides the city centre we naturally also visited Wawel Castle. In the catacombs of the cathedral that stands within its precinct, some of the Polish kings and important later figures of Polish history are buried.

After the visit to Kraków we planned to move on to Biskupin, where our overnight stay awaited us. On the way, however, there were several Slavic hillforts. Of these we visited the very fine peninsula hillfort of Bnin. The peninsula projecting into Lake Bnińskie was occupied in three phases in prehistory and the Middle Ages. At the turn of the Bronze Age and the Early Iron Age this position, suitable for defence, was used by the people of the Lusatian culture, who settled in the southern part (which at that time was an island offshore). The second time the site was intensively occupied was in the 840s, when a strongly fortified early Piast fortress was built here. It was in use (with an interruption of 160 years) right down to the beginning of the 13th century. As can be seen in the photographs from the archaeological excavation, the hillfort had the typical grillage construction, and in its lower part the so-called hooks were used, which is a typical element of Polish hillforts. In the middle of the 13th century a dwelling for the castellans was built on the base of an ancient burial mound. In 1386–1395 Bnin was granted a town charter based on Magdeburg law.
